-118.40700,34.06830.name: Southern California Reproductive Center
-118.40700,34.06830.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: Mark W. Surrey, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

-96.71958,17.07621.name: Instituto Vida Instituto De Ciencias En Reproduccion Humana
-96.71958,17.07621.desc: A clinic mapped in OpenStreetMap as offering fertility treatment. OpenStreetMap holds what somebody chose to map, so a country with few points here may be thinly mapped rather than thinly served. That is the reverse of the national registers alongside it, which are close to complete for one country and silent everywhere else. This layer is a cross-check and a source of leads, not a count.

-122.27286,37.87084.name: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
-122.27286,37.87084.desc: An organisation accredited by AAALAC International for its care and use of laboratory animals. Accreditation is voluntary and paid for, so this is a list of organisations that chose to be inspected rather than a register of everyone doing the work. An organisation absent from it is not accredited; that says nothing about whether it uses animals. In several countries the largest users are absent for exactly that reason. The directory gives a city and country and no street address, so this point marks where the organisation is registered rather than the building where animals are held.

-122.27286,37.87084.name: University of California, Berkeley
-122.27286,37.87084.desc: An organisation accredited by AAALAC International for its care and use of laboratory animals. Part of University of California. Accreditation is voluntary and paid for, so this is a list of organisations that chose to be inspected rather than a register of everyone doing the work. An organisation absent from it is not accredited; that says nothing about whether it uses animals. In several countries the largest users are absent for exactly that reason. The directory gives a city and country and no street address, so this point marks where the organisation is registered rather than the building where animals are held.

-0.50152,51.64266.name: Dr Himanshu Borase
-0.50152,51.64266.desc: A fertility clinic licensed and inspected by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority. Satellite clinic to IVF London. A satellite is where patients are seen; the licence sits with the parent clinic, so the regulator's paperwork and the treatment are in different places. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. The HFEA licenses every clinic in the United Kingdom, inspects them, and publishes findings and success rates clinic by clinic. No other fertility regulator publishes at this level, which makes the UK the one country where this sector can be read rather than estimated.

-97.16279,49.90815.name: Canadian Science Centre for Human and Animal Health
-97.16279,49.90815.status: Certificate of GAP Last visit: regular, March 2025
-97.16279,49.90815.desc: An institution certified by the Canadian Council on Animal Care for its use of animals in science. A site of Canadian Food Inspection Agency. Certificate of GAP Last visit: regular, March 2025. CCAC certification is a condition of federal research funding rather than a licence, so an institution outside it is not necessarily outside the work — it may simply not take federal money. The CCAC publishes names and certificate status and no addresses, so this point marks the institution rather than the building where animals are held.

-55.50972,-11.86122.name: LabFIV Sinop
-55.50972,-11.86122.desc: A centre accredited by REDLARA, the Latin American Network of Assisted Reproduction. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. REDLARA accreditation is voluntary and its members report to a shared registry, which is why Latin America can be read at all — most countries in the region have no national register of clinics. What it is not is a complete list: a clinic outside REDLARA appears nowhere.

-1.22000,51.71800.name: Oxford Nanopore Technologies
-1.22000,51.71800.state: Oxford — Gosling Building, Edmund Halley Rd
-1.22000,51.71800.desc: Handheld sequencers that work outside a laboratory, running on a laptop and reading long stretches of DNA in real time. They were used to track Ebola in Guinea in 2015 and Zika in Brazil, sequencing outbreak samples where they were collected rather than shipping them to a distant institute — which changes who holds the data and how fast a response can begin. The same portability makes verification possible in the other direction: a field-usable sequencer means a grower, a customs officer or a campaigner can check what is in a sample without asking anyone's permission.

-97.74310,30.26720.name: GloFish
-97.74310,30.26720.desc: Fluorescent aquarium fish, the first engineered animal sold to the public anywhere, now a routine pet-shop product. Established populations have since been found in Brazilian streams, having spread from ornamental fish farms. The pathway that mattered was never the aquarium — it was the farm supplying them, and nobody was monitoring it because a decorative pet was not treated as an environmental question. They were created at the National University of Singapore in the late 1990s as living pollution indicators, with work done on making them fluoresce selectively in the presence of toxins, before the marketing rights were taken up and they were sold as pets.

-97.74310,30.26720.name: Crestview Genetics
-97.74310,30.26720.desc: The company founded to clone one polo player's horses, after tissue was preserved from a mare that had to be put down following a fracture in a tournament final in 2006. It partnered with a Texas cloning firm to do the work, and the first foals were born in 2010. At the end of that year a clone of the player's flagship mare sold at auction for a reported $800,000. This is the clearest illustration in the facet of what drives the market: not agricultural yield, not conservation, but the resale value of a copy of a single exceptional animal — and a sport whose governing bodies had to decide afterwards whether the copies could compete.

-74.03000,40.74200.name: Modern Meadow
-74.03000,40.74200.desc: Produces collagen by fermentation with engineered yeast for use in leather alternatives. Collagen is an animal protein made without an animal, which puts it outside both the agricultural rules and the medicines rules that would otherwise cover a protein of that kind.
